vignette:
Mark is a 49-year-old plumber who, for the last eighteen months, has felt like he is living in the shadow of a past he cannot escape. The trauma was not a single event but the culmination of a two-year relationship with his former partner, which ended after a final, brutal assault. The incident that broke him began quietly. His ex, who had a volatile temper, had become enraged over a perceived slight. The argument started with a low, simmering anger that Mark had learned to dread more than shouting. As his ex's fury grew, a pan of oil left on the stove began to smoke, filling their small apartment with an acrid, burning smell just as the violence began. That specific sensory detail-the odor of scorching oil combined with the sight of barely-contained rage-became inextricably linked to the physical pain and terror that followed.

In the years since leaving that relationship and marrying his wife, Sarah, Mark believed he had moved on. He built a stable life and a successful small business. But lately, the past has been intruding with increasing force. Certain cues in his environment now trigger a cascade of fear that feels as immediate as the original threat. The smell of burnt food from a neighbor's barbecue or toast left too long in the toaster can send a jolt of alarm through him, making his heart pound. This visceral reaction is most disruptive at work. Last month, while on a job, a homeowner began to express calm but firm anger about the final invoice. For Mark, the man's stern expression and controlled tone were a terrifying echo of his ex-partner's demeanor just before an outburst. In that moment, the client's garage felt as dangerous as his old apartment.

These triggers have come to dictate Mark's behavior, leading him to construct an ever-shrinking world in an effort to feel safe. After the encounter with the angry client, Mark found he couldn't stop replaying the man's face in his mind, which in turn brought back unwanted images from the assault. To combat this, he has developed a rigid habit of avoidance; he now works late into the night organizing his truck or doing paperwork, anything to occupy his mind and stave off the memories that crowd in when he is still. He makes wide, inefficient detours on his plumbing routes to avoid driving through the entire west side of the city, where he and his ex once lived. The thought of even seeing the building from a distance is enough to cause a wave of nausea.

The most entrenched of these new habits is his relationship with sleep. The quiet darkness of the bedroom has become a threatening space where the intrusive thoughts are most powerful. To manage this, Mark stays up long after Sarah has gone to bed, watching television with the volume low until he is so exhausted he can no longer keep his eyes open, hoping to fall into a dreamless sleep the moment his head hits the pillow. This pattern has created a chasm in his marriage; Sarah feels his distance and worries about his exhaustion, but any attempt she makes to discuss it is met with a placating response. He cannot bear even the mildest confrontation, fearing that any expression of frustration could escalate. He feels he is failing her, but the alternative-facing the memories in the dark-feels impossible. It was after Sarah found him asleep on the sofa for the third time in a week, her face a mixture of concern and quiet hurt, that Mark finally called to make an appointment. He came to therapy not knowing how to explain the fear, only knowing that his strategies for survival are now dismantling the very life he fought so hard to build.
